title: Research
text: My research aims to make the hospital a place where people with opioid use disorder (OUD) receive effective treatment and stay connected to care after they leave. Fentanyl has changed what withdrawal looks like, how patients respond to standard medication starts, and how often they leave the hospital before treatment is complete. I use real-world clinical data, mixed methods, and implementation science to understand those gaps and to test practical, systems-level fixes.

title: Research
text:
Current focus
Withdrawal management in the fentanyl era. Opioid withdrawal is often undertreated in the hospital, and it is a common reason patients leave before treatment is complete. I am interested in how improvements to EHR-based clinical decision support could strengthen opioid withdrawal management, and I contributed to a 2026 consensus meeting on how opioid withdrawal should be measured.
Methadone and buprenorphine in the hospital. I study how methadone dosing during hospitalization relates to patient-directed discharge and readmission, and how buprenorphine and methadone initiation have changed for patients using fentanyl.
Patient-directed discharge. Leaving the hospital before treatment is complete is common among people with OUD and is associated with serious harm. My work examines its drivers and the hospital practices that can reduce it.
Data systems and policy. Hospitals often cannot confirm a patient’s methadone dose from their opioid treatment program. I have worked on integrating opioid treatment program data into Maryland’s health information exchange (CRISP), presented this work to the Maryland Health Services Cost Review Commission, and co-led a national workshop on methadone dose confirmation under federal privacy rules (42 CFR Part 2).

Support and recognition
My research has been supported by an NIH/NCATS KL2 award through the Johns Hopkins Institute for Clinical and Translational Research, the Johns Hopkins Center for Innovative Medicine Next Generation Scholars Award, and a Johns Hopkins Department of Medicine CORE Coins Award. I am a Research in Addiction Medicine Scholar (2025–2027) and a fellow of the Center for Dissemination & Implementation Science at Stanford (C-DIAS). In 2025 I was named Researcher of the Year by the Johns Hopkins Division of Hospital Medicine, and in 2026 I received the College on Problems of Drug Dependence Community Champion Award.

About Me
I am a hospitalist and addiction medicine physician at Johns Hopkins, where I am an Assistant Professor of Medicine in the Divisions of Hospital Medicine and Addiction Medicine. I care for hospitalized patients at The Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, including on the inpatient substance use disorders consult service, and I teach medical students and residents. I am board certified in internal medicine and addiction medicine.
My research focuses on improving hospital care for people with opioid use disorder in the fentanyl era: how we manage withdrawal, how we start and dose methadone and buprenorphine, why patients leave the hospital before treatment is complete, and what systems-level changes help them stay connected to care. My work has been supported by an NIH KL2 career development award through the Johns Hopkins Institute for Clinical and Translational Research, a Center for Innovative Medicine Next Generation Scholars Award, and the Research in Addiction Medicine Scholars program. Earlier in my career I used real-world data to study emerging issues in COVID-19 and mpox, including the safety of Paxlovid in pregnancy and risk factors for severe mpox.
I am originally from Durham, North Carolina. I graduated from Yale, earned my MD and MPH at the University of North Carolina, and moved to Baltimore in 2016 for internal medicine residency at Johns Hopkins. In 2024 I completed an MHS through the Graduate Training Programs in Clinical Investigation (GTPCI) at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
You can find more about my research and my CV on this site. Please feel free to contact me if you would like to discuss potential projects.
